title: Design a Chat System (WhatsApp / Messenger)
tagline: Real-time 1:1 and group messaging with delivery guarantees, presence, and offline delivery.
summary: WebSocket connection servers, message routing, delivery + offline.

blocks.title: Functional
items: 1:1 messaging in real time; group chats (small groups).
Message persistence + history; offline users receive messages on reconnect.
(Out of scope: media details, E2E encryption internals, calls.)

blocks.title: Non-functional
items: Highly available; reliable delivery (no lost messages).
Scale to hundreds of millions of concurrent connections.

paragraphs: Chat needs the server to *push* messages to clients, so we use persistent **WebSocket** connections (long-lived, full-duplex). Because connections are stateful, we dedicate a tier of **connection servers (gateways)** whose only job is to hold open WebSockets — each can hold tens to hundreds of thousands of connections (bounded by memory/file descriptors).

A user connects to one connection server (via a load balancer that supports long-lived connections). We record *which server holds which user* in a **presence/registry** store (e.g., Redis: `user_id → connection_server`), updated on connect/disconnect with heartbeats to detect drops.

blocks.caption: Users hold WebSockets on connection servers; a registry maps user→server; a message bus routes between servers.

items.title: A sends to its connection server
items.detail: User A's message arrives over its WebSocket to, say, connection server 1.

items.title: Persist first
items.detail: Server 1 writes the message to the durable message store (so it's never lost) and assigns it a sequence id for ordering.

items.title: Find B's server
items.detail: Look up recipient B in the presence registry → B is on connection server 7 (or offline).

items.title: Route via the bus
items.detail: Server 1 forwards the message to server 7 through the pub/sub message bus; server 7 pushes it down B's WebSocket. Send A a 'sent' ack; when B's device acks, send a 'delivered' receipt.

items.title: If B is offline
items.detail: Store the message as undelivered (per-user inbox/queue); when B reconnects, deliver the backlog and mark delivered.

blocks.title: Persist-then-deliver
blocks.text: Always durably store the message *before* attempting delivery. That way a crash mid-delivery never loses it — on reconnect the client syncs anything it's missing. Delivery is best-effort on top of a durable log.

paragraphs: The message store is write-heavy and queried by 'recent messages in a conversation' — a textbook **wide-column NoSQL** (Cassandra/HBase) case. Partition by `conversation_id` (or chat_id) and cluster by message sequence/timestamp descending, so fetching the latest messages in a chat is a single efficient partition read, and pagination scrolls back through the partition.

**Ordering**: global ordering across a distributed system is hard and unnecessary; you only need ordering *within a conversation*. Assign each message a per-conversation sequence number (or a time-sortable id) so clients can order and detect gaps. Since one conversation's messages share a partition, this is natural.

blocks.title: Don't store the messaging firehose in SQL
blocks.text: At billions of messages/day, a single SQL primary can't absorb the write volume, and you don't need joins on the hot path. Wide-column NoSQL partitioned by conversation gives the write throughput and the exact read pattern you need. (User accounts/auth can still live in SQL.)

items.detail: Clients send periodic heartbeats; the connection server updates 'last seen' in Redis with a TTL. No heartbeat → considered offline. Broadcasting presence to all contacts is expensive — fan out lazily or only to open chats.

For small groups, fan out the message to each member's connection (look up each member's server, route, persist per member or once per conversation). Large groups (broadcast channels) move toward a fan-out-on-read model like feeds.
A user may have several connections (phone + web). The registry maps user→{servers}; deliver to all devices and sync read state across them.
Add connection servers; balance by connection count. The presence registry and pub/sub bus must scale (sharded Redis / partitioned topics).
On reconnect, the client sends its last-seen sequence id per conversation; the server streams everything after it. This sync-on-reconnect makes delivery robust to drops.

blocks.text: The arc to deliver: 'WebSocket connection servers + a presence registry (user→server) + a pub/sub bus to route between servers; persist every message in wide-column storage partitioned by conversation, ordered by per-conversation sequence; queue for offline users and sync on reconnect.' That's a complete senior answer.

cheatsheet: Use WebSockets on a dedicated connection-server tier (stateful, long-lived); balance by connection count.
Presence registry (Redis: user→connection server) + pub/sub bus to route a message from sender's server to recipient's server.
Persist-then-deliver: durably store every message before pushing, so crashes never lose messages.
Store messages in wide-column NoSQL partitioned by conversation_id, clustered by sequence/time (single-partition recent reads).
Order per-conversation with a sequence id (no need for global order); offline users get a queue + sync-on-reconnect by last-seen id.
Presence via heartbeats + TTL; small groups fan-out per member, huge broadcast groups use fan-out-on-read.

questions.prompt: User A (on connection server 1) sends a message to user B who is offline, then comes online 10 minutes later. Trace how B reliably receives it.
questions.hint: Persist first; queue for offline; sync on reconnect.
answer: When A's message reaches connection server 1, the server first **persists** it durably to the message store (assigning a per-conversation sequence id) and acks 'sent' to A. It then looks up B in the presence registry and finds B offline. So it writes the message to B's **undelivered queue/inbox** (or simply relies on the persisted conversation log plus B's last-delivered pointer). No delivery attempt is lost because the message is durably stored.

Ten minutes later B reconnects to some connection server and sends its **last-seen sequence id** for that conversation (or globally). The server streams all messages after that id — including A's — pushes them to B, and marks them delivered (triggering a 'delivered' receipt back to A). This persist-then-store-then-sync-on-reconnect flow guarantees reliable, ordered delivery despite B being offline and despite any server crashes in between.
keyPoints: Persist message durably + sequence id before anything
B offline → enqueue / rely on persisted log + last-delivered pointer
On reconnect, B sends last-seen id; server streams everything after
Mark delivered + send receipt to A; nothing lost via persist-first
followUps: How do you keep read/delivered state consistent across B's phone and laptop?

questions.prompt: Why do you need a presence registry and a pub/sub bus instead of connection servers talking directly?
questions.hint: Server 1 doesn't hold B's socket — how does it even know where B is?
answer: Any user's WebSocket lives on exactly one (or a few) connection servers, and the sender's server generally doesn't hold the recipient's socket. The **presence registry** (user→connection server, in Redis) is how the sender's server discovers *which* server currently holds the recipient's connection — without it, server 1 has no way to find B among hundreds of servers.

The **pub/sub bus** is how server 1 actually hands the message to server 7 (B's server) so it can push it down B's socket. Hard-wiring direct connections between every pair of connection servers would be an O(N²) mesh that's brittle and doesn't scale; a message bus (or per-server topic) decouples them — server 1 publishes to B's server's channel, server 7 consumes and delivers. Together, registry + bus let an arbitrary sender reach an arbitrary recipient across a large, dynamic fleet.
keyPoints: Recipient's socket is on a different server; sender must locate it
Pub/sub bus routes the message to the right server (delivery)
Avoids O(N²) direct mesh; decoupled + scalable
followUps: What happens to the registry entry if a connection server crashes?
